title: Basic tools
author: Minute-Picture9006
selftext: Well, I’m basically developing a trading strategy that can’t be easily implemented using traditional rule-based code. While doing some research, I came across this Reddit community, and I was wondering if someone could help me figure out which tools I should use to start adapting my strategy into an AI-powered trading bot.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
before tools, write down what the strategy actually decides on, even if it's fuzzy. if you can't name the inputs, a model can't learn them either, it'll just fit noise and look brilliant in a backtest.

practically: python and pandas for the data, scikit-learn before anything deep, and a broker sandbox to run it on. the step people skip is letting it trade fake money for a few weeks after the backtest looks good. that last step is what Quantradin does, I built it: no real money, costs nothing, and a bot places orders on it through an API. quantradin.com.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: Writing down the inputs first is the right order, and starting with scikit-learn before anything deep keeps it testable. One thing I'd add is making sure every input is timestamped as of when it would have been known, since look-ahead leaks are the usual reason a model looks brilliant in a backtest. Also compare it to a simple rule baseline, because if the model can't beat that out-of-sample, it isn't adding anything. Cymetica's EventTrader (event timing for earnings and macro releases) is one example of an input source with that kind of point-in-time timing.

comments.author: Careless-Rent-4903
comments.body: first define what the AI is predicting. next return direction probability TP hits before SL or asset ranking are very different problems. I'd start with sklearn/lightgbm then feed predictions into a proper backtester like nautilus or vectorbt pro and test thresholds with fees and slippage. split everything by time and purge overlapping labels. bots fail usually from bad labels and leakage not lack of GPU

comments.author: AcanthocephalaNo6605
comments.body:
You basically need 2 layer architecture

1) mathematical model of strategy which can trade  
2) AI monitor which can tweak strategy in accepted range to adopt to market condition

You can utilize [while25](https://while25.com) for this. Its programmable trading platform where you can define strategy in algorithm and setup monitor which can run every one to five minutes change strategy if market conditions are changed

Connect your broker account there and you are ready to go.

comments.author: Mundane_Cicada_1427
comments.body:
If you're already comfortable with Python, I'd start there rather than jumping straight into an "AI trading bot" framework.

I'd separate the project into a few pieces: market data → feature engineering → model training → backtesting → execution. For the ML part, start with something like XGBoost before going anywhere near deep learning. It's much easier to understand what the model is actually learning.

Also, one important thing: if your strategy is difficult to express as rules, first figure out *what information a human is using to make the decision*. Things like market structure, volatility, price location, time of day, previous highs/lows, etc. Those become features for the model.

The hardest part usually isn't getting an ML model to make predictions. It's creating a dataset and backtest that don't accidentally leak future information.

comments.author: pemakenemi56
comments.body: What part of the strategy actually needs AI? If you can define the inputs and the decision you’re trying to make, you may not need an LLM at all. I’d probably separate it into data collection → signal generation → execution first, then only use a model for the part that’s genuinely fuzzy/unstructured.
